nameStory: American water-pennywort gets its charming name from its tiny, round leaves that look just like miniature pennies floating on or near water. The "water" part is obvious since it loves wet places, while "pennywort" comes from the old English word for penny, referring to any plant with small, coin-shaped leaves.
description: American water-pennywort is a delicate, low-growing plant that hugs the ground or floats in shallow water. This tiny member of the ivy family produces clusters of perfectly round leaves, each about the size of a dime or penny, attached to thin, creeping stems. The plant rarely grows taller than a few inches, instead spreading horizontally to form small mats in wet areas. Its inconspicuous white flowers are so small you might miss them entirely.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Perfectly round, coin-sized leaves with a smooth, waxy feel and shallow scalloped edges. Each leaf is attached at its center like a tiny green umbrella, giving it a distinctive peltate appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, creeping mats that hug wet soil or float on shallow water. Stems are thin, smooth, and often reddish, sprawling horizontally rather than growing upright.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers clustered in small, inconspicuous groups that are easy to overlook. Each flower is smaller than a pinky nail and appears in summer.

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Always found in wet places - look for it at pond edges, in shallow water, or in perpetually moist soil that squelches underfoot.

habitat: American water-pennywort thrives in consistently wet environments throughout New England's lowlands and mountains. You'll find it creeping along pond edges, in shallow water of marshes and swamps, and in boggy areas where the soil stays perpetually moist. It particularly loves spots where water levels fluctuate, sometimes growing as a floating plant and other times as a ground-hugger on wet mud.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green and tender, beginning the plant's active growing season. The creeping stems start to spread and establish new patches.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with the most abundant foliage and tiny white flowers appearing. This is the best time to spot and identify the plant when leaves are at their largest and most numerous.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn reddish or bronze before dying back. The plant begins to slow its growth as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to underground parts in most areas, though it may persist as dormant stems in protected, warmer microclimates near water.

funFact: Despite being called a water plant, American water-pennywort is actually in the same family as English ivy - you can see the family resemblance in how both plants spread with creeping stems, though one climbs up trees while the other hugs wet ground!
confusionNotes: The round, centrally-attached leaves make this plant quite distinctive, but beginners might confuse it with young water lily leaves. Remember: water lily leaves are much larger, often have a slit from edge to center, and float on deeper water, while pennywort leaves are tiny, complete circles found in shallow areas.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name "pennywort" fool you into thinking this has anything to do with actual pennies or currency - it's purely about the coin-like leaf shape. Also, while it shares the "pennywort" name with several other Hydrocotyle species, American water-pennywort is the most widespread native species in our region.
compareHints: American water-pennywort can be distinguished from its relatives by its consistently round leaves and preference for the northeastern climate. Manyflower marshpennywort has leaves that are more deeply lobed rather than simply scalloped, while floating marsh pennywort (rarely found here) has kidney-shaped rather than perfectly round leaves. The round, shield-like leaves of American water-pennywort are its signature feature among the genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's water pennyworts, manyflower marshpennywort has the most perfectly circular leaves and the most obvious umbrella-shaped flower clusters.
Among New England's pennyworts, whorled pennywort is the easiest to identify because of its perfectly circular leaves attached at the center.
Unlike American Water-pennywort which has kidney-shaped or lobed leaves, Sibthorp's Pennywort has perfectly round, unlobed leaves.
Unlike its pennywort relatives in New England, floating marsh pennywort is the only one that forms true floating mats on open water.
**[UNCERTAIN]** Compared to its more common cousin American Water-pennywort, this species likely differs in leaf size, flower arrangement, or specific habitat requirements.
